title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction: The page finishes the general setup and begins the first example. Euler seeks space curves y(x), z(x) that make ∫V dx extremal, where V = V(x, y, z, p, p') and p = y', p' = z'. Write dV = M dx + N dy + N' dz + P dp + P' dp'. The Euler–Lagrange equations are N dx = dP and N' dx = dP'. On the previous page he showed that these give dV = M dx + d(pP + p'P'). So with S = V − pP − p'P' one gets a third equation, M dx = dS, i.e. d/dx(V − p V_p − p' V_p') = V_x. He remarks that any one of the three equations follows from the other two, but the third is often very useful in calculation. Problem I asks for the curve that extremizes ∫ x dy dz/dx = ∫ x p q dx (he renames p' as q). Then V = pqx, so M = pq, N = N' = 0, P = qx, P' = px and S = −pqx. The three equations are pq dx = −d(pqx), 0 = d(qx), 0 = d(px). The last two integrate at once to qx = a, px = b. The next page finishes the solution: y = f + b ln x, z = g + nb ln x with n = a/b, so z = ny + c. Both projections are logarithmic curves, but the whole curve lies in one plane. Euler notes that this example therefore does not properly belong to the non-planar topic, though it shows how the method reveals when the extremal is planar.
errors: The printed differential reads ∂V = pq∂x + px∂p + px∂q. The second term should be qx∂p, since ∂V/∂p = qx. This is a typographical slip only: the collated values P = qx and P' = px are correct, and so are all later results.

Gap (not an algebraic error): Euler says the integral takes a 'maximum or minimum'. But the integrand x p q is bilinear in (p, q), so the second variation 2∫ x δp δq dx is indefinite for x > 0. The extremal is therefore a saddle, neither a maximum nor a minimum. Euler does not discuss this, which is standard for the period.

ideas.what: Auxiliary first-integral-type equation M dx = dS with S = V − pP − p'P', valid for several dependent functions; it is redundant given the Euler–Lagrange equations but useful in calculation
ideas.modern_name: Du Bois-Reymond / Erdmann first integral (Beltrami identity when V does not depend on x; Hamiltonian H = p·V_p − V with dH/dx = −∂V/∂x)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler for one dependent variable (Methodus inveniendi, 1744); the Beltrami identity is often attributed to Beltrami (1868); the corner/Erdmann form to Erdmann (1877)
ideas.where_published: E65 Methodus inveniendi (1744), for one dependent function; the several-variable form was standard after Lagrange's δ-method

ideas.what: Euler–Lagrange equations for a functional of two unknown functions (space curves): N dx = dP, N' dx = dP'
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Lagrange system for several dependent variables
ideas.where_published: E65 and Euler's later variational papers (e.g. Institutiones calculi integralis vol. III appendix); Lagrange 1760–61

ideas.what: Example ∫ x y' z' dx: the momenta x y' and x z' are conserved, giving logarithmic projections and a planar extremal (z = ny + c)
ideas.modern_name: Cyclic coordinates / conserved momenta; recognizing degenerate (planar) extremals

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds a routine general identity Euler already knew, plus a simple worked example that turns out to be planar. Nothing appears absent from the literature beyond a misprint and the standard unverified 'max/min' claim.
transcription_corrections: The transcription silently corrects the printed differential. The original actually reads '∂V = pq∂x + px∂p + px∂q', with a misprint for qx∂p.
